title: Testing Equivalent Expressions with Desmos Sliders
description: Learn a fast, reliable way to answer "which expression is equivalent?" questions in two or more variables: give each variable a Desmos slider, pick random values, and let the numbers pick the matching answer choice.

blocks.html:
Match it, don't expand it

Some SAT questions hand you a messy expression with two or more variables — like \(3a(2a-b)+b(a+5)\) — and ask which answer choice is equivalent. You could expand everything by hand and risk a sign slip. Or you could let Desmos do the checking.

By the end of this lesson you'll be able to give each variable a slider, plug in random numbers, and quickly find the one answer choice that matches — even when the variables are \(x\) and \(y\).

Let's start by watching the idea in action. The original expression is \(a(2b+3)\). Two "answer choices" are also loaded: \(2ab+3a\) and \(2ab+3\).

The sliders are set to \(a=2\) and \(b=3\). When every variable already has a value, Desmos shows an expression's value right after an equals sign. Look at the number Desmos prints for each row.

Tip: Drag the \(a\) and \(b\) sliders to new numbers and watch which row keeps matching the original.

content.prompt: With \(a=2\) and \(b=3\), the original \(a(2b+3)\) shows \(18\). Which choice also showed \(18\)?
content.explanation: \(2ab+3a = 2(2)(3)+3(2) = 12+6 = 18\), matching the original. The choice \(2ab+3\) forgot to distribute the \(a\) to the \(3\), so it only reached \(15\).

blocks.html:
Here's why that works. Two expressions are equivalent when they are just different-looking versions of the same thing.

Key idea: Equivalent expressions always produce the same output from the same input. Feed both the same numbers and you'll get the same value — every time.

So if a choice ever gives a different number than the original, it can't be equivalent. And the one choice that keeps matching for your test numbers is the answer.

content.hint: Think about what the word 'equivalent' promises. Does it hold for just one lucky value, or always?
content.prompt: For two expressions to be truly equivalent, their values must match…
choices: for at least one input you pick
content.explanation: Equivalent means same output for every input. That's exactly why plugging in numbers works: if a choice disagrees on your test values, it's out.

blocks.html:
The process

Turn that idea into a repeatable routine you can run on test day:

  1. Type the original expression into Desmos.
  2. Add a slider for each variable (Desmos offers this automatically).
  3. Set the sliders to different random values — not \(0\) and not \(1\).
  4. Type each answer choice until one shows the same value as the original. That's your answer.

Why avoid \(0\) and \(1\)? Because those values make too many different expressions accidentally agree, and you could pick the wrong choice.

Watch out: At \(a=1, b=1\), both \(2ab\) and \(a+b\) equal \(2\) — yet they're not equivalent. At \(a=2, b=3\) they split apart: \(12\) versus \(5\).

Random, boring numbers like \(2\) and \(3\) keep the imposters from hiding.

content.prompt: You test the choices using \(a=1\) and \(b=1\). Two different choices both equal the original. What should you do?
choices: Pick whichever of the two matched expressions looks simpler — both must be equivalent
Conclude that none of the four expressions is actually equivalent to the original
Re-test with other values like \(a=2, b=3\), since \(0\) and \(1\) often make different expressions match
Set both variables to \(0\) instead and see whether the same two choices still match
content.explanation: A tie at \(1\) (or \(0\)) usually means the test values were too friendly. Switch to different, non-trivial numbers and the imposter will break away from the original.

blocks.html:
Watch one all the way through

Original: \(a(3a+2b)-2b(a-b)\). The choices are loaded below with \(a=2\) and \(b=3\). Read each value:

  • \(a(3a+2b)-2b(a-b) = 30\) (the original)
  • \(3a^2+2b^2 = 30\)  — matches!
  • \(3a^2-4ab+2b^2 = 6\)
  • \(3a^2+2ab+2b^2 = 42\)

Only \(3a^2+2b^2\) matches. Notice the middle \(ab\) terms in the original cancel — easy to miss by hand, impossible to miss with sliders. Drag \(a\) and \(b\) to confirm the match holds.

content.hint: Type each choice into the calculator with \(p=2, q=3\) and read the value after the equals sign. Only one shows \(45\).
content.prompt: Try one yourself. The original is \(2p(3p-q)+q(4p+q)\). Use the calculator with \(p=2, q=3\) (original value \(=45\)). Which choice is equivalent?
content.explanation: \(6p^2+2pq+q^2 = 24+12+9 = 45\), the only match. The \(-2pq\) version drops to \(21\), and the others miss too — the numbers decide it for you.

calculator.title: Test each choice at p = 2, q = 3

blocks.html:
One catch: the letters \(x\) and \(y\)

Desmos treats lowercase \(x\) and \(y\) as the graphing axes, so it won't hand you sliders for them. If your question uses \(x\) and/or \(y\), just retype them as capital \(X\) and \(Y\).

Key idea: Capital \(X\) and \(Y\) are ordinary variables to Desmos — it will give them sliders like any other letter. Change every \(x\to X\) and \(y\to Y\), in the original and in every choice.

(One limit of the method: if a question has no answer choices to test, there's nothing to match against — this trick won't help there.)

content.prompt: The question uses variables \(x\) and \(y\), but Desmos won't create sliders for them. What's the fix?
choices: Replace \(x\) and \(y\) with capital \(X\) and \(Y\) everywhere, then add sliders
Give up on using sliders, since the method cannot handle questions written with \(x\) and \(y\)
Set \(x=0\) and \(y=0\), compare the values once, and keep whichever choice matches
Create one shared slider and use its value for both \(x\) and \(y\) in every choice
content.explanation: Capital \(X\) and \(Y\) act like normal variables in Desmos, so they get sliders. Swap them in the original and in every choice, then test as usual.

content.prompt: Transfer task. Which expression is equivalent to \(4x(x-2y)+3y(2x+y)\)? Use the calculator: retype the variables as \(X\) and \(Y\), give them sliders (they start at \(X=2, Y=3\)), and test each choice.

calculator.title: Test the choices (use capital X and Y)

blocks.html: Exactly. Typing \(4X(X-2Y)+3Y(2X+Y)\) at \(X=2, Y=3\) gives \(31\), and only \(4X^2-2XY+3Y^2\) also gives \(31\). The \(-8xy\) and \(+6xy\) combine to \(-2xy\).

Not quite — that's a sign or combining slip. Expanding gives \(4x^2-8xy+6xy+3y^2\), and \(-8xy+6xy=-2xy\), not \(-14xy\) or \(+14xy\). Numerically, \(4X(X-2Y)+3Y(2X+Y)=31\) at \(X=2, Y=3\); test each choice and only one hits \(31\).
The safest move is always the same: sliders on random numbers, then match the value. No hand-expanding required.

content.prompt: Recall the routine. Before you start typing answer choices, what must you do so Desmos gives fair, trustworthy results?
choices: Set every variable's slider to \(0\) so the arithmetic stays as simple as possible
Set each variable to \(1\), since multiplying by \(1\) cannot change an expression's value
Give each variable a slider and set them to different values other than \(0\) or \(1\)
Give a slider to just one of the variables and leave the other letters fixed at their defaults

blocks.html: Right. Every variable gets a slider, and you set them to distinct, ordinary numbers like \(2\) and \(3\) — never \(0\) or \(1\), which let imposters sneak through.

Careful — \(0\) and \(1\) are exactly the values to avoid, because different expressions often coincide there. Give each variable its own slider and choose different, non-trivial numbers so only the true match survives.
That's the whole tool: original in, sliders on random values, type choices, match the number.

content.html:
You've got it

For any "which is equivalent?" question in two or more variables: type the original, slider every variable, set random values (not \(0\) or \(1\)), and match the value. If the variables are \(x\) and \(y\), switch them to capital \(X\) and \(Y\) first. Let the numbers pick your answer.
